RC circuits and the time constant
Written for the Margin evaluation corpus. Released under CC0.
Charging a capacitor
When a capacitor C is connected through a resistor R to a battery of voltage V0, current flows and
charge builds up on the plates. The current is largest at the start, when the capacitor is empty and
the whole battery voltage appears across the resistor, and it falls as the capacitor voltage rises.
Kirchhoff's voltage law gives the differential equation V0 = R dq/dt + q/C, whose solution for an
initially uncharged capacitor is
V(t) = V0 (1 - e^(-t/RC))
The product RC has units of seconds and is called the time constant, written tau. After one time
constant the capacitor has reached 63.2 percent of its final voltage. After five time constants it has
reached 99.3 percent, which is why engineers treat a circuit as settled after about 5 tau.

Discharging and energy
A charged capacitor discharging through a resistor follows V(t) = V0 e^(-t/RC): after one time
constant the voltage has fallen to 36.8 percent of its starting value. The time to fall to half is RC ln
2, about 0.69 tau.
The energy stored in a capacitor charged to voltage V is one half C V squared. When a capacitor is
charged from a battery through a resistor, exactly half of the energy the battery supplies is
dissipated as heat in the resistor, whatever the value of R. A smaller resistor charges the capacitor
faster but dissipates the same total energy with a higher peak current.
Example: a 10 microfarad capacitor charged through a 100 kilohm resistor has a time constant of 1
second. Charged to 9 volts it stores 0.405 millijoules.

The RC low-pass filter
Taking the output across the capacitor turns the circuit into a first-order low-pass filter. At low
frequencies the capacitor's impedance is large and the output follows the input; at high frequencies
the capacitor shorts the signal to ground. The cutoff frequency, where the output power falls to half
and the amplitude to 1/sqrt(2) of the input, is
f_c = 1 / (2 pi R C)
Above the cutoff the response falls by 20 decibels per decade of frequency, and the phase shift
approaches 90 degrees. Swapping the resistor and capacitor, so that the output is taken across the
resistor, gives a high-pass filter with the same cutoff frequency.
The same time constant governs both views of the circuit: a filter with a cutoff of 159 hertz has RC
equal to 1 millisecond, so its step response settles in about 5 milliseconds.

How glaciers move
Written for the Margin evaluation corpus. Released under CCO.
A glacier forms where more snow falls each winter than melts each summer. Buried snow is
compressed into firn, granular ice that has survived at least one melt season, and over
decades the firn becomes dense glacier ice.
The upper part of a glacier, where snowfall exceeds melting over a year, is the
accumulation zone. The lower part, where melting and sublimation exceed snowfall, is the
ablation zone. The boundary between them is the equilibrium line, and its altitude is a
sensitive indicator of climate: when summers warm, the equilibrium line altitude rises and
the glacier shrinks.
Glaciers move in two ways. Internal deformation is the slow creep of ice crystals under the
glacier's own weight, fastest near the surface. Basal sliding happens when meltwater at the
bed lubricates the contact between ice and rock, and it can make a glacier surge many
times faster than its normal speed.
Rock debris carried by the ice is dropped where the ice melts. Ridges of this debris along
the sides of a glacier are lateral moraines, and the ridge left at the glacier's furthest
advance is the terminal moraine.

Thin lenses
Written for the Margin evaluation corpus. Released under CC0.
A thin converging lens brings parallel rays to a focus at its focal point, a distance f from the lens.
For an object at distance d_o from the lens, the image forms at distance d_i given by the thin lens
equation
1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i
The lateral magnification is m = -d_i / d_o. A negative magnification means the image is inverted.
When the object is further than 2f from the lens, the real image is smaller than the object; between f
and 2f it is larger; at exactly 2f the image is the same size and also at 2f on the other side.
An object inside the focal length, closer than f, gives a negative d_i: the image is virtual, upright and
magnified, on the same side as the object. That is how a magnifying glass works.
Example: an object 30 cm from a lens of focal length 10 cm forms a real, inverted image 15 cm
behind the lens, half the size of the object.
